title: Structure of Atom
summary: Rutherford fired α-particles at a thin gold foil. Most passed straight through, a few were deflected through large angles, and about 1 in 8000 bounced back.

Conclusions (the nuclear model): (1) most of the atom is empty space; (2) all the positive charge and almost all the mass are concentrated in a tiny central nucleus (about 10⁻¹⁵ m, against an atom of about 10⁻¹⁰ m); (3) electrons revolve round the nucleus, with the electrostatic attraction providing the centripetal force.
The distance of closest approach of an α-particle scattered back through 180° gives an upper estimate of the nuclear radius.
Drawbacks: by classical theory a revolving electron should radiate energy and spiral into the nucleus, so atoms would be unstable and give continuous spectra.
## Bohr's model of the hydrogen atom

Postulates: (1) electrons move only in certain stationary orbits without radiating; (2) in these orbits the angular momentum mvr = nh/2π (h/2π in the ground state); (3) radiation is emitted or absorbed only when the electron jumps between orbits: hν = E₂ − E₁.

Results: the orbit radius rₙ = n²a₀, with a₀ = 0.53 Å, so the third orbit is 9a₀ and r₂ : r₁ = 4 : 1. The energy Eₙ = −13.6/n² eV, giving −13.6, −3.4 and −1.51 eV for n = 1, 2, 3. The ratio of the first and second excited states is E₂ : E₃ = 9 : 4.
The ionization energy of hydrogen is 13.6 eV; for hydrogen-like He⁺ it is 13.6Z² = 54.4 eV.
Lyman series: n₁ = 1, ultraviolet. Balmer: n₁ = 2, visible (e.g. 4861 Å, 6563 Å). Paschen: n₁ = 3, infrared. Brackett: n₁ = 4. Pfund: n₁ = 5, far infrared.
The shortest wavelength comes from the largest energy jump (e.g. 6 → 1). The longest Paschen line (4 → 3) is λ = 144/7R. The transition 3 → 1 gives 1/λ = 8R/9, i.e. λ ≈ 102.6 nm (Lyman).
From level n the maximum number of spectral lines is n(n − 1)/2; for n = 4 it is 6.
The maximum number of electrons in the outermost shell of any atom is 8.

vsa: Write two postulates of Rutherford's atomic model.

(1) All the positive charge and nearly all the mass of an atom are concentrated in a tiny central nucleus.
(2) Electrons revolve round the nucleus in orbits, the electrostatic attraction providing the centripetal force; most of the atom is empty space.
Calculate the ratio of the energies of hydrogen in its first excited state and its second excited state.

Eₙ = −13.6/n². First excited state n = 2: −3.4 eV. Second excited state n = 3: −1.51 eV.
E₂ : E₃ = (1/4) : (1/9) = 9 : 4.

(1) Electrons revolve in certain stationary orbits without radiating energy.
(2) In these orbits the angular momentum is an integral multiple of h/2π: mvr = nh/2π.
(3) Energy is emitted or absorbed only when an electron jumps between orbits: hν = E_i − E_f.
What were the drawbacks of Rutherford's model?

A revolving electron is accelerated, so by classical theory it should radiate energy continuously and spiral into the nucleus. Atoms would be unstable and would give a continuous spectrum — contrary to observed stable atoms and line spectra.
sa: A hydrogen atom makes a transition from n = 3 to n = 1. Find the wavelength emitted and name the series. (R = 1.097 × 10⁷ m⁻¹)

1/λ = R(1/1² − 1/3²) = R × 8/9 = 1.097 × 10⁷ × 0.889 = 9.75 × 10⁶ m⁻¹.
λ ≈ 1.026 × 10⁻⁷ m = 102.6 nm.
The final level is n = 1, so it belongs to the Lyman series (ultraviolet).
Describe Rutherford's α-scattering experiment and its conclusions.

A narrow beam of α-particles from a radioactive source was directed at a thin gold foil; a zinc-sulphide screen detected the scattered particles at various angles.
Observations: most passed undeviated; a few were deflected through large angles; about 1 in 8000 bounced back.
Conclusions: the atom is mostly empty; its positive charge and mass are in a tiny nucleus (about 10⁻¹⁵ m); electrons revolve round it.
Name the series of the hydrogen spectrum with their regions and the formula for each.

1/λ = R(1/n₁² − 1/n₂²):
Lyman — n₁ = 1, ultraviolet.
Balmer — n₁ = 2, visible.
Paschen — n₁ = 3, infrared.
Brackett — n₁ = 4, infrared.
Pfund — n₁ = 5, far infrared.
In each series n₂ = n₁ + 1, n₁ + 2, …
la: Using Bohr's postulates, show that the energy of the electron in the nth orbit of hydrogen is Eₙ = −13.6/n² eV.

Centripetal force from electrostatic attraction: mv²/r = ke²/r² … (1)
Quantum condition: mvr = nh/2π … (2)
From (1) and (2): rₙ = n²h²/(4π²mke²) = n² × 0.53 Å, and v = 2πke²/nh.
KE = ½mv² = ke²/2r; PE = −ke²/r.
Total E = −ke²/2r = −2π²mk²e⁴/(n²h²).
Substituting the constants: Eₙ = −13.6/n² eV (−13.6 eV for n = 1, −3.4 eV for n = 2).
